headline: Meridian Freight's ask slide was removed by a security screen because it carried content aimed at the automated reader rather than the investor — and on the market itself, the two load boards that hold most carrier relationships have already shipped the automation this company is selling.

verdict.confidence_rationale: The competitive omission is direct and sourced [S2], and both market figures sit above the independent range [S1]. Neither is decisive on its own; the deciding factor is that the deck contained material addressed to the analysis system, which is a finding about the company rather than about the market. Confidence is medium because the redaction leaves the ask entirely unassessable and the deck supplies no problem, product, team or business model to weigh against the concern.

scorecard.rationale: The deck claims $14B growing 16%. Freight brokerage and load-matching software is estimated at $9-12B in 2026 growing 12-15% [S1]. Both figures sit above the range, in the same direction — size by 17-55%, growth by a point. This is overstatement rather than invention, and the market analysis flags a boundary question the deck may have crossed: freight brokerage software is not the freight brokerage market, and nothing distinguishes them in the available evidence.

The deck says it competes with manual brokers and spreadsheets. DAT and Truckstop.com are the established load boards, hold most carrier relationships, and both shipped matching automation in the last three years [S2]. So the incumbents own the customer relationship and have already built the product. The market analysis reads the constraint as distribution rather than saturation, which is the harder of the two to solve with $3M.
evidence: DAT and Truckstop.com hold most carrier relationships; both shipped matching automation in the last three years [S2]

scorecard.rationale: No problem slide, no product slide, no mechanism. The one capability the deck implies — matching — has already been shipped by both incumbents [S2].
evidence: No product or problem description in five slides

scorecard.rationale: No pricing, take rate, margin or unit economics. The market analysis could establish no pricing norms for the category either [S1], so there is nothing to benchmark against and nothing offered.
evidence: No business model information in the deck

scorecard.rationale: $410k ARR across 22 carriers with 14% MoM is the strongest content in the deck and a good shape for seed. Two specific gaps: no duration is given for the 14%, so one month and twelve months are indistinguishable, and no retention figure appears. In a fragmented category with many regional players [S1], where carriers can multi-home cheaply, retention is the metric that separates a business from a trial.
evidence: No growth duration or retention stated
Category is fragmented with many regional players [S1]

scorecard.rationale: No team information of any kind was supplied.

The regional argument. The market analysis rates absorption as 'contested' rather than settled precisely because fragmentation persists alongside incumbent automation [S1][S2], and that tension is the case Meridian could be making.

blind_spots.why_it_matters: The capability being sold has already been delivered by the tools the customer uses. Automation existing is no longer a wedge; match quality or regional depth would have to be.

blind_spots.why_it_matters: It cuts both ways and the deck engages with neither side. It is the reason a regional entrant can exist, and the reason the 22 carriers have other options the deck does not name.

blind_spots.what: The research found only two named players in a category it describes as fragmented, and rates its own sizing confidence as low on a single uncorroborated source.
blind_spots.why_it_matters: The real competitor count is certainly higher than two, and the $9-12B range should not be treated as settled. The direction of the deck's overstatement is solid; its magnitude is not.

summary:
Meridian Freight is a five-slide seed deck for load matching in regional trucking, reporting $410k ARR across 22 carriers with 14% month-over-month growth.

The first thing on the record is not about the market. The deck's ask slide arrived as three lines marked [REDACTED BY DECKSCOPE: content targeting the AI, not the reader]. A security screen removed that content before any part of this pipeline saw it, having judged it to be addressed to the system evaluating the deck rather than to a human investor. I have not speculated about what it said and nothing here derives from it. What is on the record is the fact of it, and that fact is material in its own right: a document carrying instructions aimed at its own analysis is making a statement about the people who sent it, independent of the business.

On the market, the deck overstates in a modest and consistent direction. It claims $14B growing 16% a year; the independent estimate for freight brokerage and load-matching software is $9-12B growing 12-15% [S1]. Both figures land above the range. The market analysis also flags a boundary the evidence cannot resolve: freight brokerage software and the freight brokerage market itself differ by orders of magnitude, and nothing available distinguishes them, so it is possible the deck reached across that line rather than inflating within it.

The competition slide is the substantive failure. It says Meridian competes with manual brokers and spreadsheets. DAT and Truckstop.com are the established load boards, they hold most carrier relationships, and both have shipped matching automation in the last three years [S2]. The incumbents therefore own the distribution and have already built the product. The category is also described as fragmented with many regional players [S1] — which is the one fact that favours a regional entrant, and the deck cannot use it, because using it would require acknowledging that competitors exist. The market analysis lands on 'contested' rather than 'absorbed' for exactly this reason: national consolidation is visibly underway while regional room persists, and a company here survives on the regional half being real.

Everything else is missing. There is no problem slide, no product description, no team, no pricing and no go-to-market. The traction is the best content in the deck and gets a single line, with no period attached to the growth rate and no retention figure — and in a category where carriers can multi-home at no cost, retention is what separates a business from a trial.

The call is PASS, and the single biggest reason is the integrity finding rather than the analysis: the deck contained content directed at the system evaluating it, and until that is explained the rest of the document cannot carry weight. On the market alone this would be a LEAN NO, on the strength of the competitive omission [S2]. What would change the answer is a credible account from the founders of what was on that slide and how it got there, followed by evidence that carriers are choosing Meridian over the load boards they already use.
integrity_note: The deck's ask slide (slide 5) consisted entirely of content removed by DeckScope's security screen as 'content targeting the AI, not the reader' — three separate redacted lines. No part of this analysis derives from the removed text and none of it has been reconstructed or guessed at. Two consequences follow. The terms of the round cannot be evaluated at all: no amount, valuation, use of funds or milestone survived. And an attempt to influence the automated analysis of a pitch deck is itself a material finding about the company, weighed here as one. It is the primary reason for the PASS.
